**Problem.** Let $G$ be a finite group, $S, T \in \mathrm{Syl}_p(G)$ distinct, with $|S \cap T|$ maximal among all such intersections. Prove $N_G(S \cap T)$ has no normal Sylow $p$-subgroup.

---

**Proof.**

Set $D = S \cap T$. Since $S \neq T$ and $|S| = |T|$ (both Sylow), $D \subsetneq S$ and $D \subsetneq T$; otherwise $S \leq T$ and equal orders force $S = T$, contradiction.

We use a standard fact: **in a finite $p$-group $P$, every proper subgroup $H$ satisfies $H \subsetneq N_P(H)$.** *(Proof by induction on $|P|$: $Z(P) \neq 1$. If $Z(P) \not\leq H$, then $Z(P) \leq N_P(H) \setminus H$, done. If $Z(P) \leq H$, pass to $P/Z(P)$ and apply induction to $H/Z(P)$.)*

Applying this:
$$D \subsetneq N_S(D), \qquad D \subsetneq N_T(D). \tag{1}$$

Note $D, N_S(D), N_T(D)$ are all $p$-subgroups contained in $N_G(D)$: $D \leq N_G(D)$ since $D$ normalizes itself; $N_S(D) \leq N_G(D)$ since elements normalizing $D$ within $S$ also normalize $D$ in $G$; likewise $N_T(D)$.

**Suppose for contradiction** that $N_G(D)$ admits a normal Sylow $p$-subgroup $P$. Then $P$ is the *unique* Sylow $p$-subgroup of $N_G(D)$, so every $p$-subgroup of $N_G(D)$ lies in $P$. In particular:
$$D \leq P, \quad N_S(D) \leq P, \quad N_T(D) \leq P. \tag{2}$$

Now $P$ is a $p$-subgroup of $G$, so $P \leq S'$ for some $S' \in \mathrm{Syl}_p(G)$.

**Claim: $S' = S$.** From (2), $N_S(D) \leq P \leq S'$, and also $N_S(D) \leq S$, so $N_S(D) \leq S \cap S'$. By (1), $|N_S(D)| > |D|$. If $S' \neq S$, then $S \cap S'$ is an intersection of two *distinct* Sylow $p$-subgroups with
$$|S \cap S'| \geq |N_S(D)| > |D| = |S \cap T|,$$
contradicting the maximality of $|S \cap T|$. Hence $S' = S$, i.e., $P \leq S$.

**Claim: $S' = T$.** Identically, $N_T(D) \leq P \leq S'$ and $N_T(D) \leq T$, so $N_T(D) \leq T \cap S'$. By (1), $|N_T(D)| > |D|$. If $S' \neq T$, then $|T \cap S'| > |D|$, again contradicting maximality. Hence $S' = T$, i.e., $P \leq T$.

Combining both claims: $P \leq S \cap T = D$. Together with $D \leq P$ from (2), we get $P = D$.

But then $N_S(D) \leq P = D$, i.e., $N_S(D) \leq D$. Since always $D \leq N_S(D)$, this gives $N_S(D) = D$, **contradicting** (1), which says $D \subsetneq N_S(D)$.

This contradiction shows that $N_G(D) = N_G(S \cap T)$ cannot have a normal Sylow $p$-subgroup. $\blacksquare$
